title: LEA: Improving Sentence Similarity Robustness to Typos Using Lexical Attention Bias

problem.claim: Textual noise such as typos and abbreviations harms vanilla Transformers on downstream tasks, including sentence similarity.

gap.claim: Existing data-augmentation approaches remain vulnerable to token distribution shifts induced by typos.

contributions.claim: The work equips sentence-similarity cross-encoders with a LExical-aware Attention module that incorporates lexical similarities between words in both sentences.
LEA improves robustness to textual noise across product matching, textual entailment, and paraphrasing settings.
The work analyzes several LEA design choices and reports their impacts.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe the LExical-aware Attention module as novel.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments with three Transformer encoders on five e-commerce product-matching datasets show consistent performance gains under noise while remaining competitive on clean splits.
Evaluations on two textual-entailment and paraphrasing datasets report robustness to typos in longer-sentence, more natural-context domains.
The authors report that LEA helps cross-encoders handle complex noisy-text scenarios, especially for short descriptions with limited context.

narrative_sequence.summary: Textual noise penalizes Transformer-based downstream tasks and affects sentence similarity.
Cross-encoders model sentence-pair interrelations, while prior robustness methods mainly use data augmentation but remain affected by token distribution shifts.
LEA adds lexical-similarity information as an attention bias to cross-encoders.
Experiments report gains under noise across product matching, entailment, and paraphrasing while retaining competitiveness on clean data.
The work examines design choices and their reported impacts.

source_observation.claim: The approach uses raw-text lexical similarities to avoid tokenization shifts caused by typos.

interpretation.claim: Robustness may improve when noise-sensitive processing is supplemented with signals computed before tokenization.

application.claim: For noisy short-text matching, consider incorporating character- or word-level similarity signals into token-based cross-encoders.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether the same approach is effective for noise types other than typos or abbreviations.

source_observation.claim: LEA is reported as effective in both short-text product matching and longer-context entailment and paraphrasing datasets.

interpretation.claim: The reported robustness may extend across substantially different sentence lengths and task contexts.

application.claim: Evaluate robustness methods across both compact domain-specific text and longer natural-language sentence-pair tasks.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify the noise levels, baselines, statistical tests, or per-dataset results.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the LEA architecture, training procedure, or lexical-similarity computation.
The abstract does not provide quantitative results, noise levels, baselines, or statistical significance.
The abstract does not identify which design choices were analyzed or their individual effects.
